--- title: "From Linear Regression to Deep Learning: Your First Neural Network" description: "What a weight really is, why a single neuron is just linear regression, and how hidden layers and depth let a network learn curves. Interactive, step by step." author: "MLStation" date: 2026-10-01 categories: [ML, Deep Learning] draft: false --- Deep learning sounds mysterious, but its building block is something you already know: **multiply inputs by weights, add them up**. That is linear regression. A neural network simply stacks many of these small calculations in **layers**, with a bend (an *activation*) in between. Stack enough layers and you have **deep learning**. ::: {.callout-tip} ## What you will learn - What a neuron and a **weight** are, with a live diagram - Why one neuron with no bend **is** linear regression, weight by weight - How a hidden layer lets the model learn a curve linear regression cannot - How an ANN and a deeper DNN solve a five-feature problem - How to **save** the trained model and load it again ::: ## The building block: one neuron A neuron takes inputs $x_1, x_2, \dots$, multiplies each by its own **weight**, adds a **bias**, then passes the total through an **activation function** $f$: $$ z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + w_3 x_3 + b, \qquad a = f(z) $$ {#eq-neuron} ::: {.callout-important} ## What is a weight, exactly? A **weight** is a single number attached to one connection. It answers one question: **if this input goes up by 1, how much does it push the neuron's total $z$, and in which direction?** - **Large** weight: the input matters a lot. **Near zero**: the input is almost ignored. - **Positive** weight: the input pushes the total **up**. **Negative**: it pushes it **down**. - The **bias** $b$ is the starting value before any input is added. Think of each weight as a volume knob on one microphone: it sets how loud, and with what sign, that input is heard. Training means turning all the knobs until the predictions match the data. ::: Play with the knobs. Line thickness shows the **size** of each weight, colour shows its **sign**. ```{ojs} //| echo: false import {ms, msStyle} from "/assets/js/ms-plot.js" viewof x1 = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 1.0, step: 0.1, label: "Input x₁"}) viewof x2 = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Input x₂"}) viewof x3 = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: -1.0, step: 0.1, label: "Input x₃"}) viewof w1 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 2.0, step: 0.1, label: "Weight w₁"}) viewof w2 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: -1.0, step: 0.1, label: "Weight w₂"}) viewof w3 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0.3, step: 0.1, label: "Weight w₃"}) viewof bias = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0.0, step: 0.1, label: "Bias b"}) viewof act = Inputs.radio(["none (linear)", "ReLU", "sigmoid"], {value: "ReLU", label: "Activation f"}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false neuron = { const xs = [x1, x2, x3], ws = [w1, w2, w3]; const z = d3.sum(xs, (x, i) => x * ws[i]) + bias; const a = act === "ReLU" ? Math.max(0, z) : act === "sigmoid" ? 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-z)) : z; const W = 640, H = 270, cx = 400, cy = 135; const ys = [55, 135, 215]; const col = w => w >= 0 ? ms.indigo : ms.rose; return htl.svg`` } html`
z = (${w1})(${x1}) + (${w2})(${x2}) + (${w3})(${x3}) + (${bias})${(w1*x1 + w2*x2 + w3*x3 + bias).toFixed(2)}
` ``` **ReLU** (rectified linear unit) is the most common activation: it outputs $\max(0, z)$, so it is zero until the total crosses zero, then rises in a straight line. That one bend is what gives neural networks their power. ## Weights vs linear regression Linear regression with one feature is $\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$. Now look at a neuron with one input and **no activation**: $\hat{y} = b + w\,x$. Same formula, different names. | | Linear regression | Neural network | |---|---|---| | Multiplier on an input | Coefficient $\beta_1$ (slope) | Weight $w$ | | Constant term | Intercept $\beta_0$ | Bias $b$ | | How it is found | One exact formula (least squares) | Gradual adjustment (gradient descent) | | Meaning of the multiplier | Fixed effect of $x$ everywhere | Effect of $x$ **on one neuron**; the total effect depends on all neurons | | Can it bend? | No, always a straight line | Yes, once a hidden layer with activation is added | | Number of parameters | Features + 1 | Can be thousands or billions | : Weights in linear regression vs a neural network {#tbl-compare} ## Experiment 1: one feature, one target A building's electricity demand depends on the outside temperature. Below about 22 °C demand is flat. Above it, the air conditioning turns on and demand climbs. We simulate 120 days. ::: {#setup-1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Simulate 120 days of temperature and demand"} import numpy as np, pandas as pd, warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_absolute_error import plotly.graph_objects as go from ms_charts import COLORS, PLOTLY_CONFIG rng = np.random.default_rng(7) n = 120 temp = rng.uniform(5, 40, n) # °C cool = np.maximum(temp - 22, 0) # air conditioning kicks in at 22 °C demand = 50 + 2.6 * cool + 0.04 * cool**2 + rng.normal(0, 3, n) # kW x = temp.reshape(-1, 1) grid = np.linspace(5, 40, 200) ``` ::: ### Model A: linear regression vs a single neuron We fit ordinary linear regression, then train **one neuron with no activation** using gradient descent: start with $w = 0, b = 0$, measure the error, nudge both numbers downhill, and repeat. ::: {#09fda0e6 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Train both models"} lr = LinearRegression().fit(x, demand) # a single neuron trained by gradient descent (on scaled x for stability, then converted back to °C) mu, sd = temp.mean(), temp.std() z = (temp - mu) / sd w, b, eta, path = 0.0, 0.0, 0.1, [] for epoch in range(80): pred = w * z + b err = pred - demand path.append(dict(epoch=epoch, w=w / sd, b=b - w * mu / sd, mse=float((err**2).mean()))) w -= eta * 2 * (err * z).mean() # gradient of mean squared error w.r.t. w b -= eta * 2 * err.mean() # gradient w.r.t. b w_neuron, b_neuron = w / sd, b - w * mu / sd ``` ::: ::: {#8d7b4588 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Drag the slider to watch the neuron learn. Its line starts flat at zero and settles exactly on the linear regression line. ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof ep = Inputs.range([0, 79], {value: 0, step: 1, label: "Training step"}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false cur = path[ep] html`
Neuron weight w${cur.w.toFixed(3)}bias b${cur.b.toFixed(2)}Regression slope ${ols.w.toFixed(3)}, intercept ${ols.b.toFixed(2)}
` ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Plot.plot({ ...msStyle, height: 340, x: {label: "Temperature (°C) →", domain: [5, 40]}, y: {label: "↑ Demand (kW)", domain: [-5, 110]}, marks: [ Plot.dot(pts1, {x: "t", y: "y", r: 3, fill: ms.slate, fillOpacity: 0.55}), Plot.line([5, 40].map(t => ({t, y: ols.b + ols.w * t})), {x: "t", y: "y", stroke: ms.amber, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "6,4"}), Plot.line([5, 40].map(t => ({t, y: cur.b + cur.w * t})), {x: "t", y: "y", stroke: ms.indigo, strokeWidth: 3}), Plot.text([{t: 6, y: 104}], {x: "t", y: "y", text: () => "solid: neuron dashed: linear regression", textAnchor: "start", fill: "currentColor", fontSize: 12}) ] }) ``` ::: {#ae68ab35 .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=4} | Parameter | Linear regression | Single neuron | Same? | |---|---|---|---| | Slope / weight | 1.644 | 1.644 | Yes | | Intercept / bias | 26.79 | 26.79 | Yes | | R² | 0.758 | 0.758 | Yes | ::: ::: **Similarity:** with no hidden layer and no activation, the neuron's weight **is** the regression slope and its bias **is** the intercept. Both say "each extra degree adds about 1\.64 kW, everywhere". **Difference:** regression solves it in one exact step, the neuron gets there by trial and correction. Both are wrong in the same way: the data bends, a straight line cannot. ### Model B: add a hidden layer with two ReLU neurons Now we put **two hidden neurons** with ReLU between the input and the output: $$ \hat{y} = v_1\,\text{ReLU}(w_1 x + b_1) + v_2\,\text{ReLU}(w_2 x + b_2) + c $$ {#eq-ann1} ::: {#1ceab3dd .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Train the 1-2-1 network"} ann1 = MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(2,), activation="relu", solver="lbfgs", max_iter=5000, random_state=5).fit(z.reshape(-1, 1), demand) W1 = ann1.coefs_[0][0] / sd # input-to-hidden weights in °C units B1 = ann1.intercepts_[0] - ann1.coefs_[0][0] * mu / sd # hidden biases V, C = ann1.coefs_[1].ravel(), float(ann1.intercepts_[1][0]) # hidden-to-output weights and bias hinge = -B1 / W1 # temperature where each neuron switches on/off parts = [V[j] * np.maximum(W1[j] * grid + B1[j], 0) for j in range(2)] r2_ann1 = r2_score(demand, sum(V[j] * np.maximum(W1[j] * temp + B1[j], 0) for j in range(2)) + C) ``` ::: ::: {#aae8326d .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Each hidden neuron draws one **hinge**: flat on one side, a straight slope on the other. The output adds the hinges together. Toggle them to see how the curve is built. ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof show = Inputs.checkbox(["Neuron 1 × v₁", "Neuron 2 × v₂", "Network output"], {value: ["Network output"], label: "Show"}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Plot.plot({ ...msStyle, height: 340, x: {label: "Temperature (°C) →"}, y: {label: "↑ kW"}, marks: [ Plot.dot(pts1, {x: "t", y: "y", r: 3, fill: ms.slate, fillOpacity: 0.45}), show.includes("Neuron 1 × v₁") ? Plot.line(parts, {x: "t", y: "n1", stroke: ms.amber, strokeWidth: 2.5}) : null, show.includes("Neuron 2 × v₂") ? Plot.line(parts, {x: "t", y: "n2", stroke: ms.rose, strokeWidth: 2.5}) : null, show.includes("Network output") ? Plot.line(parts, {x: "t", y: "total", stroke: ms.indigo, strokeWidth: 3.5}) : null, Plot.ruleX([kink], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.3, strokeDasharray: "4,4"}) ] }) ``` Now compare the parameters **weight by weight**: ::: {#9ea457e8 .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=7} | Parameter | What it does | Value | Linear regression equivalent | |---|---|---|---| | $w_1$, $b_1$ | Hidden neuron 1: switches at 22.3 °C | -0.77, 17.2 | None | | $w_2$, $b_2$ | Hidden neuron 2: switches at 4.7 °C | 0.42, -2.0 | None | | $v_1$, $v_2$ | How strongly each hinge counts in the output | 4.45, 7.99 | None | | $c$ | Output bias | -10.3 | Like the intercept | | **Total** | | **7 parameters** | **2 parameters** | | **R²** | | **0.978** | **0.758** | ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## The key difference In linear regression, the slope is **one number** that applies at every temperature. In the network, **no single weight is "the slope"**. The slope below 22 °C is $v_1 w_1 + v_2 w_2 \approx$ \-0\.10 kW per °C (flat), and above it is 3\.35 kW per °C. The network **discovered the air-conditioning threshold** near 22 °C without being told. That is the trade: more flexible, less directly readable. ::: ## Experiment 2: five features, one target Real buildings depend on more than temperature. We simulate 3,000 hourly readings with five features: | Feature | Meaning | |---|---| | `temp` | Outside temperature (°C) | | `humidity` | Relative humidity (%) | | `hour` | Hour of day (0 to 23) | | `weekend` | 1 on Saturday and Sunday | | `occupancy` | People in the building | ::: {#4ad245d5 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Simulate 3,000 hourly readings"} N = 3000 F = pd.DataFrame({ "temp": rng.uniform(-5, 40, N), "humidity": rng.uniform(20, 90, N), "hour": rng.integers(0, 24, N), "weekend": (rng.random(N) < 2 / 7).astype(int), }) F["occupancy"] = rng.uniform(0, 200, N) * (1 - 0.7 * F.weekend) def true_demand(t, h, hr, wk, occ): open_ = ((hr >= 8) & (hr < 19)).astype(float) * (1 - wk) # office open on weekdays return (60 + 0.10 * (t - 18)**2 # heating and cooling (U shape) + 0.04 * h * np.maximum(t - 24, 0) # humid heat is extra costly + 35 * open_ + 0.25 * occ * open_) # lights, computers, people y = true_demand(F.temp, F.humidity, F.hour, F.weekend, F.occupancy) + rng.normal(0, 6, N) Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(F, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0) ``` ::: Linear regression first, then a network with **one hidden layer of 8 neurons**. We scale the inputs and the target, which helps the network train reliably. ::: {#39b8ab13 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} def network(layers, seed=0): mlp = MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=layers, activation="relu", solver="lbfgs", alpha=1e-3, max_iter=3000, random_state=seed) net = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), mlp) # scale inputs return TransformedTargetRegressor(regressor=net, # scale target transformer=StandardScaler()) linreg = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr) ann = network((8,)).fit(Xtr, ytr) ``` ::: This is the map of the network we just trained: 5 inputs, 8 hidden neurons, 1 output. Hover any line to read its weight. ::: {#70d3751d .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ```{ojs} //| echo: false function drawNet(coefs, inLabels, title) { const sizes = [coefs[0].length, ...coefs.map(c => c[0].length)]; const W = 700, H = 380, padX = 110, padY = 30; const xs = sizes.map((_, i) => padX + i * (W - 2 * padX) / (sizes.length - 1)); const ysOf = n => d3.range(n).map(j => padY + (j + 0.5) * (H - 2 * padY) / n); const Y = sizes.map(ysOf); const maxW = d3.max(coefs.flat(2), Math.abs); const names = i => i === 0 ? "Input" : i === sizes.length - 1 ? "Output" : `Hidden ${i}`; return htl.svg``; } drawNet(annW.coefs, feats) ``` Blue lines are positive weights, red are negative, thicker means stronger. With 5 × 8 + 8 × 1 = 48 weights plus 9 biases, the ANN has **57 parameters**. Linear regression has **6**. ## Going deep: the DNN A **deep neural network (DNN)** is simply a network with **two or more hidden layers**. The first layer learns simple patterns (for example "it is hot" or "the office is open"), the next layer combines them ("hot **and** open"). That stacking of simple ideas into richer ones is what the "deep" in deep learning means. ::: {#8f4b48f0 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} # two hidden layers: 8 neurons, then 6 neurons dnn = network((8, 6)).fit(Xtr, ytr) ``` ::: ::: {#e8374eaf .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ```{ojs} //| echo: false drawNet(dnnW.coefs, feats) ``` ### How the three models compare ::: {#52a1c015 .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=13} | Model | Parameters | Test R² | Mean error | |---|---|---|---| | Linear regression | 6 | 0.181 | 27.2 kW | | ANN (1 hidden layer: 8) | 57 | 0.871 | 9.6 kW | | DNN (2 hidden layers: 8, 6) | 109 | 0.969 | 5.2 kW | ::: ::: Linear regression cannot capture the U-shaped temperature effect or the office switching on and off, so it explains very little. The ANN captures most of it, and the extra layer in the DNN lifts accuracy further. On a small problem like this, a wider single layer can also get close. Depth pays off most on complex data such as images, audio and text. ### Try it yourself Change the conditions and watch all three models respond. The "true" value comes from the simulation formula, without noise. ::: {#ebed2c6f .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof q = Inputs.form({ temp: Inputs.range([-5, 40], {value: 33, step: 1, label: "Temperature (°C)"}), humidity: Inputs.range([20, 90], {value: 70, step: 1, label: "Humidity (%)"}), hour: Inputs.range([0, 23], {value: 14, step: 1, label: "Hour of day"}), weekend: Inputs.toggle({label: "Weekend", value: false}), occupancy: Inputs.range([0, 200], {value: 120, step: 5, label: "Occupancy"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false predict = (m, x) => { let a = x.map((v, i) => (v - m.mean[i]) / m.scale[i]); m.coefs.forEach((M, l) => { a = M[0].map((_, j) => d3.sum(a, (v, i) => v * M[i][j]) + m.ints[l][j]); if (l < m.coefs.length - 1) a = a.map(v => Math.max(0, v)); }); return a[0] * m.ys + m.ym; } xq = [q.temp, q.humidity, q.hour, q.weekend ? 1 : 0, q.occupancy] lrPred = mLR.b + d3.sum(xq, (v, i) => mLR.coef[i] * (v - mLR.mean[i]) / mLR.scale[i]) truth = { const open = (q.hour >= 8 && q.hour < 19 && !q.weekend) ? 1 : 0; return 60 + 0.10 * (q.temp - 18) ** 2 + 0.04 * q.humidity * Math.max(q.temp - 24, 0) + 35 * open + 0.25 * q.occupancy * open; } html`
True${truth.toFixed(0)} Linear${lrPred.toFixed(0)} ANN${predict(mANN, xq).toFixed(0)} DNN${predict(mDNN, xq).toFixed(0)}kW
` ``` Set the hour to 2 (night) or switch on Weekend: the networks drop sharply, the linear model barely moves. ## Save the model and load it later Training takes time, so you save the trained model once and reuse it. With scikit-learn, `joblib` stores the whole pipeline: the scalers, every weight and every bias. ::: {#8fd88186 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} import joblib, os path = "models/building_demand_dnn.joblib" os.makedirs("models", exist_ok=True) joblib.dump(dnn, path) # save loaded = joblib.load(path) # load, any time later new_hour = pd.DataFrame([{"temp": 33, "humidity": 70, "hour": 14, "weekend": 0, "occupancy": 120}]) print(f"Saved file size: {os.path.getsize(path) / 1024:.0f} KB") print(f"Predicted demand: {loaded.predict(new_hour)[0]:.1f} kW") same = np.allclose(loaded.predict(Xte), dnn.predict(Xte)) print("Same predictions as the original:", same) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Saved file size: 10 KB Predicted demand: 174.2 kW Same predictions as the original: True ``` ::: ::: The same idea in the two most popular deep learning libraries: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Keras ```{.python filename="keras_save.py"} model.save("building_demand_dnn.keras") model = keras.models.load_model("building_demand_dnn.keras") ``` ## PyTorch ```{.python filename="torch_save.py"} torch.save(model.state_dict(), "building_demand_dnn.pt") # weights only model = DemandNet() # same architecture model.load_state_dict(torch.load("building_demand_dnn.pt")) model.eval() ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Only load files you trust `joblib`, `pickle` and older PyTorch files can run code when loaded. Never load a model file from an unknown source. ::: ## The journey in one picture ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false flowchart LR A["Linear regression
y = b + w·x"] --> B["One neuron
same thing"] --> C["Hidden layer + ReLU
ANN: learns bends"] --> D["2+ hidden layers
DNN: combines patterns"] --> E["Save with joblib
reuse anywhere"] ``` ## Summary - A **weight** is the number that says how much, and in which direction, one input pushes one neuron. - A neuron with no activation and no hidden layer **is linear regression**: weight = slope, bias = intercept. - A **hidden layer with ReLU** adds bends. No single weight is the slope any more; the effect of an input depends on which neurons are switched on. - A **DNN** stacks two or more hidden layers to combine simple patterns into richer ones. - **Save** the trained model so you can reuse it without retraining. For the full theory, see @goodfellow2016.
